source.title: Adversarial Attacks on the Interpretation of Neuron Activation Maximization
source.authors: Géraldin Nanfack; A. Fulleringer; Jonathan Marty; Michael Eickenberg; Eugene Belilovsky

record.tranche_reason: The study deliberately fine-tunes CNNs to manipulate feature-visualization outputs and reports attack outcomes. These induced changes do not test whether unmanipulated networks naturally have polysemantic neurons or whether their mixed responses share a feature.
record.gate_note: The reported visualization changes are intentionally induced by adversarial fine-tuning. They therefore are not evidence about naturally occurring polysemanticity. The paper also compares top-k visualizations with synthetic visualizations, but does not assess whether neurons count as polysemantic under those methods. Fairwashing results concern perceived bias, not the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The paper builds adversarial fine-tuning attacks that alter top-k and fairness-related neuron visualizations in AlexNet and EfficientNet. It never measures or classifies polysemantic neurons, superposition, or whether mixed responses share one feature. All visualization changes are induced on purpose. Zoom In is cited only as background on feature visualization, so the finding is neither tested nor used as a tool (closer to T6 than T4).
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors show three attacks (push-down, push-up decoy, fairwashing) that manipulate top-k feature visualization while keeping accuracy, with little evidence of whack-a-mole. They urge caution about building mechanistic interpretations on this tool.
record.recipe_differences: Uses adversarial fine-tuning to manipulate CNN feature-visualization outputs; it does not reproduce the original sources' neuron or circuit analyses.
record.method_sensitivity: The attack's visualization effects vary by layer depth: the authors report that early layers are harder to modify than later layers. Top-k and synthetic visualization also respond differently to the top-k attacks.

fits_no_version.finding: Adversarial fine-tuning replaced top-k activating images across AlexNet conv layers and an EfficientNet block with under 0.5% accuracy loss. Later layers were easier to attack (CLIP-δ 0.043 at Conv1 vs 0.249 at Conv5).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Top-k activation-maximization interpretations of CNN channels can be adversarially manipulated while preserving model accuracy.

fits_no_version.finding: After top-k attacks, synthetic feature visualizations were largely unchanged, so the two methods were decorrelated. This was judged by visual inspection only.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Synthetic and natural top-k feature visualizations can diverge for the same channel after model manipulation.

record.problems: The main experiments use pretrained AlexNet, with an EfficientNet ablation on one selected block rather than a broad architecture survey. The authors note that their whack-a-mole metrics may be imperfect; validating correspondence would require inspecting all channels. No uncertainty estimates are reported.
record.rows_left_out: Fairwashing results and model accuracy values are not included because they concern perceived bias or performance rather than the claim's versions. Figure-only examples and individual-channel illustrations are also omitted; the table gives aggregate metrics for the attack conditions.

untested.parts: Whether natural vision-model neurons respond to unrelated inputs; no polysemanticity count or classification.
Polysemanticity without capacity pressure; not studied.
Share of polysemantic neurons across architectures or activations; not measured.
Whether mixed responses share one feature; not assessed.
Polysemanticity classification under different activation ranges or scoring. The top-k vs synthetic decorrelation concerns induced manipulation, not polysemanticity labels.

record.verdict_notes: All rows correctly link to none. The values are induced attack metrics, so cannot_determine relative to any version is appropriate. The relation was changed from uses_without_test/T4 to cites_only/T6 because the study does not rely on polysemanticity as a tool.

versions.untested_parts: Whether vision-model neurons naturally respond to unrelated input categories.
Language-model MLP neurons and layer variation.
Whether superposition or capacity pressure causes polysemanticity.
Polysemanticity arising without capacity pressure from initialization, regularization, or training noise.
Natural polysemantic-neuron prevalence across activations, architectures, or regularization, and performance costs of reducing it.
Whether naturally mixed neuron responses share a feature or related job.
Whether polysemanticity classifications depend on activation range or explanation scoring; the study manipulates visualizations but does not classify polysemantic neurons.
